brief: A utensil holder with two bins that is waterproof and dishwasher safe.

requirements.evidence: Two 2-storey pieces (piece:0,0,0 and piece:1,0,0, fused) holding deep bins sized for long utensils. The open faces are capped and the joint is bolted (jointBolt:1#0,0#0). Fit and collision checks are clear. Utensils can't be shown standing in the bins because the cutlery props only lie flat.
bin:0,0,1~hex-bin-full-x2 and bin:1,0,1~hex-bin-full-x2, one in each cell.

The configurator only checks shape and fit, not whether anything holds water. I used solid-floor bins (not the drained ones), but whether they keep water in depends on the material and print settings you choose.
The configurator knows nothing about heat or dishwasher resistance. That depends entirely on the material you print in.

finish.summary: I built the utensil holder: two hex cells side by side, each two storeys tall, with a two-storey-deep bin dropped into each one. The open faces are capped and the joint between the two cells is bolted (19 parts). The fit check and the collision check both came back clear. The configurator only checks shape and fit, so I can't say the holder is waterproof or dishwasher safe. That depends on the material you print it in and how you print it. The cutlery props only lie flat and won't fit inside the bins, so the fork, spoon and knife are laid on the bench in front of the holder for staging.

lines.label: Edge cap · male, two stories tall
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
